# Unequal Probability Sampling with Replacement (UPSWR)


## How to Do Unequal Probability Sampling?

Suppose $n>1$ and we sample **with replacement**: the selection probabilities do not change after the first
draw. Let
$$
\psi_i = P(\text{select unit } i \text{ on any given draw}),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^N\psi_i=1 .
$$

Draw $n$ units with replacement (a unit may be drawn more than once). The sample $\mathcal R$ (not $\mathcal S$)
is the list of the $n$ draws, **including repeats**: for example, $n=10$, $$\mathcal R=\{D,D,D,C,C,D,C,A,B,B\}$$ 
A common choice, **probabilities proportional to size (PPS)**, with a size variable $x_i>0$ known for every unit:
$$
\psi_i = \frac{x_i}{t_x},\qquad t_x=\sum_{k=1}^N x_k .
$$

## Drawing Probabilities in Practice

```{r}
#| label: fig-pps-line
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.6
#| out-width: "85%"
set.seed(1)
psi <- c(0.10, 0.22, 0.15, 0.28, 0.25)
labels <- LETTERS[1:5]
cum <- c(0, cumsum(psi))
draws <- c(0.06, 0.35, 0.55, 0.83)

par(mar = c(3, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1), xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n",
     xlab = "", ylab = "", bty = "n")
cols <- rep(c("#dbe9fb", "#c3dbf7"), length.out = 5)
rect(cum[-6], 0.3, cum[-1], 0.7, col = cols, border = "black", lwd = 1.5)
text((cum[-6] + cum[-1]) / 2, 0.5, labels, cex = 1.4)
axis(1, at = cum, labels = round(cum, 2), cex.axis = 0.9)
points(draws, rep(0.5, 4), pch = 17, col = "firebrick", cex = 1.8)
text(draws, rep(0.82, 4), sprintf("u=%.2f", draws), col = "firebrick", cex = 0.85)
```

Divide $[0,1]$ into segments of length $\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_N$. Draw $u\sim\text{Uniform}(0,1)$ (red triangles);
the segment that $u$ falls into determines the selected unit. In R:
`sample(1:N, size = n, prob = psi, replace = TRUE)`.

## Ratios $b_i$ and the Ratio $B$

With $\psi_i=x_i/t_x$, define for every unit
$$
b_i=\frac{y_i}{x_i},\qquad B=\frac{t_y}{t_x}=\frac{\bar y_U}{\bar x_U},\qquad \bar x_U=\frac{t_x}{N}.
$$
$B=\sum x_ib_i/\sum x_i$ is the $x$-weighted mean of the $b_i$, and
$$
\bar y_U=\bar x_U\,B,\qquad t=t_x\,B .
$$
**Estimating $B$ is enough**: build $\hat B$, then multiply by $\bar x_U$ or $t_x$.

## Sampling Distribution of $b_j^*$

Let $b_j^*$ be the ratio $b$ of the unit selected on draw $j$ (the star: it is indexed by the *draw*, so it is
random, while $b_1,\ldots,b_N$ are fixed numbers). It is a discrete random variable with distribution

| Unit selected on draw $j$ | $1$ | $2$ | $\cdots$ | $N$ |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Value of $b_j^*$ | $b_1$ | $b_2$ | $\cdots$ | $b_N$ |
| Probability | $\psi_1=x_1/t_x$ | $\psi_2=x_2/t_x$ | $\cdots$ | $\psi_N=x_N/t_x$ |

Draws are with replacement, so $b_1^*,\ldots,b_n^*$ are **IID** with this distribution.

## Mean and Variance of $b_j^*$

$$
E(b_j^*)=\sum_{i=1}^N\psi_i\,b_i=\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{x_i}{t_x}\frac{y_i}{x_i}=\frac{t}{t_x}=B,\qquad
S_{b^*}^2=V(b_j^*)=\sum_{i=1}^N\psi_i(b_i-B)^2 .
$$
A single draw is unbiased for $B$, and precise when the $b_i$ are nearly equal, i.e. $y_i\propto x_i$.

## HH Estimator of $B$: Mean and Variance

The HH estimator is the mean of the $n$ IID observations $b_j^*$ (the **mean of the ratios**):
$$
\boxed{\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}}=\bar b^*=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n b_j^*},\qquad E(\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}})=B,
$$
and its variance is that of one draw divided by $n$. With $w_i=x_i/\bar x_U=N\psi_i$ (relative size),
$$
V(\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}})=\frac{S_{b^*}^2}{n}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^N\psi_i(b_i-B)^2=\frac{1}{nN}\sum_{i=1}^N w_i\,(b_i-B)^2 .
$$
No finite population correction: the draws are independent.

## Estimating the Variance; Mean and Total

The sample variance of the $b_j^*$ is unbiased for $S_{b^*}^2$:
$$
\boxed{\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}})=\frac{s_{b^*}}{\sqrt n}},\qquad
s_{b^*}^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{j=1}^n(b_j^*-\bar b^*)^2 .
$$

| Quantity | Estimate | Estimated SE |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Ratio $B=t/t_x$ | $\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}}$ | $s_{b^*}/\sqrt n$ |
| Mean per unit $\bar y_U=\bar x_UB$ | $\bar x_U\,\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}}$ | $\bar x_U\,s_{b^*}/\sqrt n$ |
| Total $t=t_xB$ | $t_x\,\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}}$ | $t_x\,s_{b^*}/\sqrt n$ |

## HH Estimator in Terms of $\psi_i$: the Weight

For any selection probabilities $\psi_i$, the HH estimator of the total is a **weighted sum** over the $n$ draws
in $\mathcal R$ (repeats included):
$$
\hat t_{\mathrm{HH}}=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\frac{y_j^*}{\psi_j^*}=\sum_{j=1}^n w_j\,y_j^*,\qquad
\boxed{w_j=\frac{1}{n\,\psi_j^*}}
$$
Unit $i$ is expected to appear $n\psi_i$ times in $\mathcal R$, so each draw of unit $i$ **represents**
$1/(n\psi_i)$ units of the population. The estimated variance is
$$
\hat V(\hat t_{\mathrm{HH}})=\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum_{j=1}^n\Big(\frac{y_j^*}{\psi_j^*}-\hat t_{\mathrm{HH}}\Big)^2 .
$$
With PPS, $\psi_i=x_i/t_x$, the weight is $w_i=t_x/(n\,x_i)$: large units get small weights.

# Comparison of the HH, Ratio and Average Estimators

## The Ratio Estimator and the Sample Average in Terms of $b_i$

With an SRS $\mathcal S$ of $n$ units, write $y_i=x_ib_i=\bar x_U\,w_ib_i$:

* **Ratio estimator** (uses $x_i$ at the estimation stage):
$$
\hat B_r=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}y_i}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}x_i}=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}x_i\,b_i}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}x_i}
$$
the mean of the sampled $b_i$ with weights $x_i$ adding up to one.

* **Sample average** (ignores $x_i$): $\bar y=\bar x_U\hat B_{\mathrm{avg}}$ with
$$
\hat B_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{\bar y}{\bar x_U}=\frac1n\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}w_i\,b_i
$$
weights $w_i$ that do not add up to one.

## Comparison of the Three Estimators of $B$ {.smaller}

| Estimator | Estimator of $B$ | $x_i$ used at | Unbiased? |
|:---|:--:|:---|:---|
| Sample average (SRS) | $\dfrac1n\sum\limits_{i\in\mathcal S}w_ib_i$ | not used | yes |
| Ratio (SRS) | $\dfrac{\sum_{\mathcal S} x_ib_i}{\sum_{\mathcal S} x_i}$ | estimation stage | slightly biased |
| HH (UPSWR) | $\dfrac1n\sum\limits_{j=1}^n b_j^*$ | design stage | exactly unbiased |

Variances (multiply by $\bar x_U^2$ for the mean, $t_x^2$ for the total):
$$
\begin{aligned}
V(\hat B_{\mathrm{avg}})&=\frac{1-n/N}{n(N-1)}\sum_{i=1}^N (w_ib_i-B)^2\\
V(\hat B_{r})&\approx\frac{1-n/N}{n(N-1)}\sum_{i=1}^N w_i^2\,(b_i-B)^2\\
V(\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}})&=\frac{1}{nN}\sum_{i=1}^N w_i\,(b_i-B)^2
\end{aligned}
$$

## Per-Unit Squared Terms

Each variance is $\frac1n\times$ the average over the units of one squared term:

| Estimator | Squared term of unit $i$ | Spread of $y$ about |
|:---|:--:|:---|
| Sample average | $(w_ib_i-B)^2$ | the flat line $\bar y_U$ |
| Ratio | $w_i^2\,(b_i-B)^2$ | the line $y=Bx$ |
| HH | $w_i\,(b_i-B)^2$ | the line $y=Bx$, weight $1/w_i$ relative to ratio |

HH divides the ratio estimator's term by $w_i$: units larger than average ($w_i>1$) are **downweighted**,
smaller ones are upweighted, because large units are already drawn more often. UPSWR wins when the large
residuals $y_i-Bx_i$ belong to the large units.

## Toy Example: Four Supermarkets, One-Draw Variances {.smaller}

$t_x=1600$, $\bar x_U=400$, $B=300/1600=0.1875$. Sales nearly proportional to floor area:

| Store | $x_i$ | $y_i$ | $w_i$ | $b_i$ | $b_i-B$ | $(w_ib_i-B)^2$ | $w_i^2(b_i-B)^2$ | $w_i(b_i-B)^2$ |
|:--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| A | 100 | 11 | 0.25 | 0.1100 | $-0.0775$ | 0.025600 | 0.000375 | 0.001502 |
| B | 200 | 20 | 0.50 | 0.1000 | $-0.0875$ | 0.018906 | 0.001914 | 0.003828 |
| C | 300 | 24 | 0.75 | 0.0800 | $-0.1075$ | 0.016256 | 0.006500 | 0.008667 |
| D | 1000 | 245 | 2.50 | 0.2450 | $0.0575$ | 0.180625 | 0.020664 | 0.008266 |
| **Variance** (Sum $/N$) | | | | | | **0.0603** | **0.00736** | **0.00557** |

HH $<$ ratio $\ll$ sample average. If the sales were unrelated to the floor area, the ordering reverses
(average $0.00078$, ratio $0.0288$, HH $0.0273$): **the size variable must be tied to $y$**.

# Computation Example: Revenue from AI Token Usage

## Setup and Sample {.smaller}

An AI company has $N=6$ customers; the tokens $x_i$ (millions) are known for all, the revenue $y_i$
(thousand dollars) is only observed for the sampled customers. Draw $n=5$ customers with replacement,
$\psi_i=x_i/t_x$ ($t_x=100$, $\bar x_U=16.67$). The sample is $\mathcal R=\{F,E,F,D,C\}$:

| Draw $j$ | Customer | $x_j^*$ | $y_j^*$ | $b_j^*=y_j^*/x_j^*$ | $b_j^*-\bar b^*$ | $(b_j^*-\bar b^*)^2$ |
|:--:|:--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1 | F | 40 | 190 | 4.7500 | $-0.1417$ | 0.020069 |
| 2 | E | 30 | 155 | 5.1667 | 0.2750 | 0.075625 |
| 3 | F | 40 | 190 | 4.7500 | $-0.1417$ | 0.020069 |
| 4 | D | 15 | 70 | 4.6667 | $-0.2250$ | 0.050625 |
| 5 | C | 8 | 41 | 5.1250 | 0.2333 | 0.054444 |
| **Sum** | | | | **24.4583** | 0 | **0.220833** |

## Estimates {.smaller}

$$
\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}}=\bar b^*=\frac{24.4583}{5}=4.8917,\qquad
s_{b^*}^2=\frac{0.220833}{4}=0.055208,\quad s_{b^*}=0.2350
$$

| Quantity | Estimate | Estimated SE |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Revenue per million tokens $B$ | $4.8917$ | $0.2350/\sqrt5=0.1051$ |
| Mean revenue per customer | $16.67\times4.8917=81.53$ | $16.67\times0.1051=1.75$ |
| Total revenue | $100\times4.8917=489.2$ | $100\times0.1051=10.5$ |

In R: `upswr_est(ydata, xdata, xbar_pop, tx_pop, method = "ratio")` with `method` equal to
`"ratio"`, `"mean"` or `"total"` returns the estimate, SE and CI.

# One-Stage Cluster Sampling with PPS

## Change of Notation

Clusters (psus) are the units: $y_i\to t_i$ (cluster total), $x_i\to M_i$ (cluster size),
$$
t_x\to M_0=\sum_{i=1}^NM_i,\qquad \bar x_U\to\bar M_U=\frac{M_0}{N},\qquad \psi_i=\frac{M_i}{M_0}.
$$
The ratio of cluster $i$ is its **mean per element (ssu-level mean)**
$$
b_i=\frac{t_i}{M_i}=\bar y_i ,\qquad B=\frac{t}{M_0}=\bar y_U\ \ (\text{mean per element}).
$$

## Estimates for One-Stage Cluster Sampling

Then $\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}}=\bar b^*=\dfrac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\bar y_j^*$: the **plain average of the sampled cluster
means** (large clusters are already selected more often), with $\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}=s_{b^*}/\sqrt n$.

| Quantity | Estimate | Estimated SE |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Mean per element $\bar y_U=B$ | $\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}}$ | $s_{b^*}/\sqrt n$ |
| Mean per cluster $t/N$ | $\bar M_U\,\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}}$ | $\bar M_U\,s_{b^*}/\sqrt n$ |
| Total $t$ | $M_0\,\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}}$ | $M_0\,s_{b^*}/\sqrt n$ |

## Computation Example: Falls in Long-Term Care Homes {.smaller}

$N=40$ homes, $M_0=3000$ residents ($\bar M_U=75$). $n=8$ draws with $\psi_i=M_i/M_0$; every resident of a
selected home is reviewed ($t_i$ = falls in the home). Home H12 is drawn twice (same $t_i$):

:::: {.columns}

:::{.column style="width:58%;"}

| $j$ | Home | $M_j^*$ | $t_j^*$ | $b_j^*=t_j^*/M_j^*$ |
|:--:|:--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1 | H12 | 180 | 160 | 0.8889 |
| 2 | H03 | 60 | 49 | 0.8167 |
| 3 | H27 | 240 | 205 | 0.8542 |
| 4 | H12 | 180 | 160 | 0.8889 |
| 5 | H31 | 95 | 70 | 0.7368 |
| 6 | H08 | 120 | 118 | 0.9833 |
| 7 | H19 | 45 | 30 | 0.6667 |
| 8 | H36 | 150 | 140 | 0.9333 |
| **Sum** | | | | **6.7688** |

:::

:::{.column style="width:42%;"}

$\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}}=6.7688/8=0.8461$ falls per resident, $s_{b^*}=0.1036$,
$\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}=0.1036/\sqrt8=0.0366$.

| Quantity | Est. | SE |
|:---|--:|--:|
| per resident | 0.846 | 0.037 |
| per home ($\times75$) | 63.5 | 2.7 |
| total ($\times3000$) | 2538 | 110 |

:::

# Two-Stage Cluster Sampling with Replacement

## Setup and Estimators

Select $n$ clusters with replacement, $\psi_i=M_i/M_0$, then take an SRS of $m_i$ elements from the cluster
**on every draw**: a cluster drawn twice gets two **independent** subsamples. The cluster mean $b_i=t_i/M_i$ is
not observed, but estimated by the subsample mean $\bar y_i$, and $\hat t_i=M_i\bar y_i$.

The one-stage formulas carry over with $\bar y_j^*$ (subsample mean of draw $j$) in place of $b_j^*$:
$$
\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}}=\bar y^*=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\bar y_j^*,\qquad
\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}})=\frac{s_{\bar y^*}}{\sqrt n},\qquad
s_{\bar y^*}^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{j=1}^n(\bar y_j^*-\bar y^*)^2 ,
$$
mean per cluster $\bar M_U\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}}$ and total $M_0\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}}$ with SEs multiplied by the same constants
(each draw estimates the total by $\hat t_j^*/\psi_j^*=M_0\bar y_j^*$).

::: {.callout-note}
**No second-stage variance formula is needed**: the draws are independent, and $s_{\bar y^*}^2$ captures both the
choice of clusters and the choice of elements within them.
:::

## Computation Example: Care Homes with Subsamples {.smaller}

Same eight draws, but $m_j^*=20$ residents are sampled per draw (15 for H19), recording their falls. H12 is
drawn twice, with different subsample means:

:::: {.columns}

:::{.column style="width:58%;"}

| $j$ | Home | $M_j^*$ | $m_j^*$ | Falls | $\bar y_j^*$ |
|:--:|:--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1 | H12 | 180 | 20 | 19 | 0.950 |
| 2 | H03 | 60 | 20 | 15 | 0.750 |
| 3 | H27 | 240 | 20 | 16 | 0.800 |
| 4 | H12 | 180 | 20 | 16 | 0.800 |
| 5 | H31 | 95 | 20 | 18 | 0.900 |
| 6 | H08 | 120 | 20 | 21 | 1.050 |
| 7 | H19 | 45 | 15 | 10 | 0.667 |
| 8 | H36 | 150 | 20 | 17 | 0.850 |
| **Sum** | | | | | **6.767** |

:::

:::{.column style="width:42%;"}

$\hat B_{\mathrm{HH}}=6.767/8=0.846$, $s_{\bar y^*}=0.120$, $\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}=0.120/\sqrt8=0.0425$.

| Quantity | Est. | SE |
|:---|--:|--:|
| per resident | 0.846 | 0.042 |
| per home ($\times75$) | 63.4 | 3.2 |
| total ($\times3000$) | 2538 | 127 |

# Unequal Probability Sampling Without Replacement (UPSWO)

## The Horvitz-Thompson Estimator

Select $n$ **distinct** units with **inclusion probabilities** $\pi_i=P(i\in\mathcal S)$, $\sum_{i=1}^N\pi_i=n$.
For $\pi$ps, $\pi_i=n\,x_i/t_x=n\psi_i$. The **Horvitz-Thompson (HT)** estimator weights each unit by $1/\pi_i$:
$$
\boxed{\hat t_{\mathrm{HT}}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}\frac{y_i}{\pi_i}}
$$
*Unbiased*: with $I_i=1$ if $i\in\mathcal S$ (and $E(I_i)=\pi_i$), $\hat t_{\mathrm{HT}}=\sum_{i=1}^N I_i\,y_i/\pi_i$ and
$$
E(\hat t_{\mathrm{HT}})=\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{y_i}{\pi_i}E(I_i)=\sum_{i=1}^N y_i=t .
$$

## Mean and Ratio from the HT Total

Mean per unit: $\hat t_{\mathrm{HT}}/N$. With $\pi_i\propto x_i$, the ratio is the HT total over $t_x$:
$$
\hat B_{\mathrm{HT}}=\frac{\hat t_{\mathrm{HT}}}{t_x}=\frac1n\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}b_i ,
\qquad \widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\hat B_{\mathrm{HT}})=\frac{\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\hat t_{\mathrm{HT}})}{t_x}.
$$

## Variances of the HT Estimator

With joint inclusion probabilities $\pi_{ij}$ (fixed sample size), **Sen-Yates-Grundy**:
$$
\hat V_{\mathrm{SYG}}=\frac12\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}\sum_{j\in\mathcal S}\frac{\pi_i\pi_j-\pi_{ij}}{\pi_{ij}}\Big(\frac{y_i}{\pi_i}-\frac{y_j}{\pi_j}\Big)^2 .
$$
Approximations that need only $\pi_i$, with $u_i=y_i/\pi_i$:

* **Hájek**: $\displaystyle\hat V_{\mathrm H}=\frac{n}{n-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}(1-\pi_i)(u_i-A)^2,\quad
A=\frac{\sum_{\mathcal S}(1-\pi_i)u_i}{\sum_{\mathcal S}(1-\pi_i)}$
* **With-replacement (WR)**: treat the sample as $n$ draws with $\psi_i=\pi_i/n$,
$\displaystyle\hat V_{\mathrm{WR}}=\frac{n}{n-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}\Big(u_i-\frac{\hat t_{\mathrm{HT}}}{n}\Big)^2$,
which ignores the factors $1-\pi_i$ and is a little too large.

For the mean divide the SE by $N$; for $\hat B_{\mathrm{HT}}$ divide by $t_x$.

## Computation Example: HT Estimate and Variances {.smaller}

$N=20$ units, a sample of $n=4$ units with inclusion probabilities $\pi_i$:

| $i$ | $y_i$ | $\pi_i$ | $u_i=y_i/\pi_i$ | $(1-\pi_i)u_i$ | $(1-\pi_i)(u_i-A)^2$ | $(u_i-\hat t_{\mathrm{HT}}/n)^2$ |
|:--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1 | 12 | 0.10 | 120.00 | 108.00 | 17.08 | 12.8 |
| 2 | 30 | 0.20 | 150.00 | 120.00 | 526.1 | 698.5 |
| 3 | 40 | 0.35 | 114.29 | 74.29 | 65.9 | 86.2 |
| 4 | 33 | 0.30 | 110.00 | 77.00 | 144.3 | 184.2 |
| **Sum** | | | **494.29** | **379.29** | **753.4** | **981.6** |

$\hat t_{\mathrm{HT}}=494.29$, mean $494.29/20=24.71$; $A=379.29/3.05=124.36$, and

$$
\hat V_{\mathrm H}=\tfrac43\times753.4=1004.5\ (\mathrm{SE}=31.7),\qquad
\hat V_{\mathrm{WR}}=\tfrac43\times981.6=1308.8\ (\mathrm{SE}=36.2).
$$
SE of the mean: $31.7/20=1.58$ (Hájek), $36.2/20=1.81$ (WR).

# When to Use UPS

## UPS Is Risky Unless $y$ Is Tied to the Size Variable

The gain depends on the ratios $b_i=y_i/x_i$ being nearly constant, i.e. $y_i$ roughly proportional to $x_i$.
Otherwise,

* the estimate can be **much worse than a plain SRS average**;
* a unit with small $x_i$ but large $y_i$ gets a huge weight $1/\psi_i$ ($1/\pi_i$), so the estimates are unstable and
  the estimated SE tends to be too small (intervals under-cover).

UPS is used mostly when the size is a good proxy of what is measured: selecting the clusters of a multi-stage
survey proportional to households or students, auditing by monetary value, surveys of establishments by
employment. If the size is only loosely related to $y$, use SRS or stratified sampling, with a ratio or
regression estimator if $x_i$ is known.

# Weights in Unequal-Probability Sampling

## General Weight Formula

For sampling **without** replacement, the weight is the reciprocal of the inclusion probability, $1/\pi_i$.
For sampling **with** replacement, we use the *first-stage* weight
$$
w_i = \frac{1}{E[Q_i]} = \frac{1}{n\psi_i},
$$
where $Q_i$ is the number of times unit $i$ occurs in $\mathcal R$. For one-stage cluster sampling, $w_{ij}=1/(n\psi_i)$
for every ssu $j$ in psu $i$, and
$$
\hat t_{\mathrm{HH}} = \sum_{i\in\mathcal R}\sum_{j=1}^{M_i} w_{ij}y_{ij}, \qquad
\hat{\bar y}_U = \frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal R}\sum_{j=1}^{M_i} w_{ij}y_{ij}}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal R}\sum_{j=1}^{M_i} w_{ij}} .
$$
For two-stage sampling with an SRS of $m_i$ ssus, the weight has the extra factor $M_i/m_i$.
